tips.title: Three types, three mechanisms
tips.body: **Solid state** uses **electrical circuits**, **magnetic** uses a **spinning magnetised disc**, **optical** uses a **laser**. Learn the mechanism for each — "explain the operation" questions want how it physically works, not what it is used for.

tips.title: No moving parts explains most SSD answers
tips.body: Faster, quieter, more durable, less power — all of it follows from **no moving parts**. Say that phrase and then the consequence, and one idea explains several advantages.

tips.title: Secondary storage is non-volatile and not directly accessible
tips.body: The definition has **two** halves: **non-volatile**, and **not directly accessible by the CPU**. Answers that give only "it keeps data when switched off" miss the part that distinguishes it from ROM.

tips.title: Cloud storage is still someone else's disc
tips.body: The specification is explicit: cloud storage uses **magnetic and/or solid state storage at a remote location**. It is not a fourth type of storage — it is the same hardware somewhere else, reached over a network.

tips.title: An embedded system does one job
tips.body: An **embedded** system is built into a device to do **one dedicated task** — a washing machine, a microwave. A **non-embedded** system, such as a laptop, is **general purpose** and runs whatever you install.

why.matters:
RAM is volatile, small and expensive, so a computer that had nothing else would lose everything the moment it was switched off and could not hold much while it was on. Secondary storage is the answer to both.

The specification defines it in two halves, and both matter: it is **non-volatile**, and it is **not directly accessible by the CPU**. The second half is the one that gets left out, and it is the one that explains why a program has to be loaded before it runs.

examples.title: Why a program has to load before it runs
examples.body:
The processor cannot reach a file on a disk. It reads and writes main memory directly and nothing else, so anything it is going to work on has to be **copied into RAM first** — which is what a loading screen is, and why opening a large file takes a moment while using it afterwards does not.

That is the half of the definition people drop. Secondary storage is non-volatile *and* not directly accessible by the CPU, and the dividing line is that accessibility, not speed and not size.

visual.alt: A table comparing main memory with secondary storage: the processor reaches main memory directly but not secondary storage, main memory is lost when the power goes, and a file has to be copied into memory before it is used

examples.title: Why a dropped laptop is the argument for solid state
examples.body:
The three types differ by **mechanism**, and the mechanism decides everything else. Magnetic storage is a head floating over a spinning platter, so a knock at the wrong moment is a scratch. Solid state has no moving parts at all, so there is nothing to jolt.

Answer a comparison question from the mechanism and the rest follows: no moving parts also means quieter, cooler and faster to reach any point, while the spinning platter is still much cheaper per gigabyte. Optical is a laser reading pits in a surface — cheap to make and post, slow, and mostly overtaken.

rows: a head on a spinning disc

visual.alt: A table of the three types of secondary storage and their mechanisms: solid state has no moving parts, magnetic uses a head over a spinning platter, and optical uses a laser reading pits and lands

examples.title: Why cloud storage is somebody else’s computer
examples.body:
Nothing new happens in the cloud. The files are on ordinary secondary storage in a building somewhere else, and what changes is that you reach them over a **network** instead of over a cable inside the case.

That single change is the whole trade. The same file is reachable from any device and somebody else does the backups — and nothing works without a connection, the speed is the network's rather than the disk's, and the data is on hardware you do not control. An exam answer that says *it is stored remotely and accessed over a network* has the definition; the rest of a good answer is in the consequences.

visual.alt: A table comparing storage on your own device with cloud storage: the cloud disk is in another building reached over a network, so it needs a connection, and the backups and the control belong to whoever owns it

steps.title: Why secondary storage exists
steps.body:
**The specification defines it carefully:**

> **Secondary storage is any non-volatile storage mechanism not directly accessible by the CPU.**

There are **two** parts to that, and both matter.

**Non-volatile** — the contents survive the power being switched off.

**Not directly accessible by the CPU** — the processor cannot reach it the way it reaches main memory. Data must be **copied into main memory** before the CPU can work on it.

**Why it is required.** Main memory is **volatile**, so everything in RAM vanishes when the machine is switched off. Without secondary storage, every file, program and setting would be gone each time. RAM is also comparatively **small and expensive**, whereas secondary storage is far larger for the money.

So a computer needs both: fast volatile memory for what it is doing **now**, and slower non-volatile storage for keeping things **permanently**.

**Note the boundary is accessibility, not speed.** Secondary storage is usually slower, but that is a consequence, not the definition — and it is why ROM, which is non-volatile but **is** directly accessible, is **not** secondary storage.

options: RAM cannot be read by the CPU without help
RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when the power is switched off
Secondary storage is faster than RAM for most tasks
RAM can only hold programs, never data files
check.solution: RAM is **volatile** — everything in it is lost at power off. Secondary storage is **non-volatile**, so files and programs survive. It is also far cheaper per gigabyte, though it is **slower**, not faster.

steps.title: The three types
steps.body:
**The specification names three, and asks you to explain the operation of each.**

**Solid state (SSD, memory card, USB stick).** Data is stored in **electrical circuits** with **no moving parts**. The specification says you need to know that SSDs use electrical circuits to persistently store data, but **not** the precise details such as NAND gates.

**Magnetic (hard disk drive, magnetic tape).** In a hard disk drive a **disc spins** while a **read-write head** moves across its surface, **magnetising** tiny areas in one direction or the other to record 0s and 1s. Mechanical, and therefore vulnerable to being knocked.

**Optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray).** Data is stored as tiny **pits** and flat **lands** on the disc surface — pressed in at the factory, or made by a **laser** on a recordable disc. To read it, a laser shines on the surface and the difference in how pits and lands **reflect** the light is read as 0s and 1s.

**The mechanism is what the question wants.** *An SSD is fast and a hard disk is slow* describes them; it does not explain how either works.

**Everything else follows from the mechanism.** No moving parts makes solid state fast, quiet, durable and low-power. Moving parts make magnetic drives cheaper per gigabyte but slower and easier to damage. Optical discs are cheap, removable and easily posted, but hold far less and scratch.

steps.title: Cloud storage and embedded systems
steps.body:
**Cloud storage** means keeping files on storage at a **remote location**, reached over a network, rather than on a device you own.

**It is not a new kind of storage.** The specification is explicit that cloud storage **uses magnetic and/or solid state storage at a remote location** — the same hardware as anything else, just somewhere else and someone else's.

**Advantages over local storage:**

- Files are reachable from **any device, anywhere** with a connection.
- **Easy to share** with other people.
- The provider handles **backups** and replacing failed drives.
- Capacity can be **increased** without buying hardware.

**Disadvantages:**

- Needs an **internet connection** — no connection, no files.
- Access is limited by **connection speed**, which is far slower than a local drive.
- **Ongoing cost**, rather than buying a drive once.
- **Security and privacy**: your data sits on someone else's hardware, and you are trusting their protection and their staff.

**Embedded systems** are the other idea in this part of the specification. An **embedded system** is a computer built **into a device** to perform **one dedicated task** — the controller in a washing machine, a microwave, or a car's engine management.

**A non-embedded system is general purpose.** A laptop or phone runs whatever software you choose to install. An embedded system does the **one job** it was built for and cannot be repurposed.

Embedded systems are usually **cheaper, smaller and more reliable** for their task, because they carry only what that task requires.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Give both halves of the definition.** Secondary storage is **non-volatile** *and* **not directly accessible by the CPU**. The second half is what separates it from **ROM**, which is non-volatile but **is** directly accessible — a question that asks why ROM is not secondary storage is testing exactly this.

**Explain operation as a mechanism.** *Data is stored as pits and lands on the disc surface, and a laser reads it by detecting the difference in reflection.* Answers that say an optical disc "stores data with a laser" have named the component without describing what it does.

**Trace every advantage back to the mechanism.** Solid state is fast, silent, durable and low-power **because it has no moving parts**. Saying the phrase once and drawing four consequences from it is worth far more than four unconnected assertions.

**Do not over-learn SSDs.** The specification states that the precise details, such as the use of NAND gates, are **not required**. Electrical circuits, persistently storing data, no moving parts — that is the level wanted.

**Say what cloud storage actually is.** It uses **magnetic and/or solid state storage at a remote location**. It is not a fourth type. That single sentence prevents the common error of treating "the cloud" as some different technology.

**Give cloud disadvantages that are not just "you need internet".** Access speed is limited by the **connection**, the cost is **ongoing** rather than one-off, and the data sits on **someone else's hardware** — a privacy and security question as much as a technical one. That last point links directly to the ethical and legal part of the specification.

**Name the cost when recommending solid state.** Magnetic storage is **cheaper per gigabyte** and offers the **largest capacities**, which is why it remains the sensible choice for bulk storage and backups. An answer that says SSDs are better in every respect is not being honest about the trade.

**Define embedded by purpose, not by size.** An embedded system does **one dedicated task**; a non-embedded one is **general purpose**. Small is not the test — a washing-machine controller is embedded, while a phone is small but general purpose, so size decides nothing.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Secondary storage** is **non-volatile** storage **not directly accessible by the CPU**.
- It is needed because **RAM is volatile**, small and expensive.
- Data must be **copied into main memory** before the CPU can use it.
- **ROM** is non-volatile but **is** directly accessible, so it is not secondary storage.
- Three types: **solid state**, **magnetic**, **optical**.
- **Solid state**: electrical circuits, **no moving parts**.
- **Magnetic**: a **spinning disc** magnetised by a moving **head**.
- **Optical**: **pits** and **lands** on the disc, read by a **laser** from how they **reflect**.
- Solid state is fastest, most durable and lowest power — all from **no moving parts**.
- **Magnetic** is cheapest per gigabyte and offers the largest capacities.
- **Optical** is cheap and very portable but holds least and scratches.
- **Cloud storage** is **magnetic and/or solid state storage at a remote location**.
- Cloud advantages: access anywhere, easy sharing, backups handled, easy to expand.
- Cloud disadvantages: needs a connection, limited by connection speed, ongoing cost, someone else's hardware.
- An **embedded system** does **one dedicated task**; a **non-embedded** system is **general purpose**.

questions.prompt: Explain what secondary storage is and why it is needed, and describe how solid state, magnetic and optical storage each work.
questions.solution:
**Secondary storage** is any **non-volatile** storage mechanism that is **not directly accessible by the CPU**. Both halves of that definition matter: ROM is also non-volatile, but the CPU **can** access it directly, so ROM is main memory rather than secondary storage.

It is **required** because main memory is **volatile** — everything in RAM is lost the moment the power goes off. Without secondary storage, every file, program and setting would disappear each time the machine was switched off. RAM is also comparatively **small and expensive**, whereas secondary storage gives far more capacity for the money. Because the CPU cannot reach it directly, data must first be **copied into main memory** before the processor can work on it.

**Solid state storage** — SSDs, USB sticks, memory cards — holds data in **electrical circuits**, with **no moving parts** at all. The specification requires knowing that SSDs use electrical circuits to persistently store data, but explicitly **not** the precise details such as the use of NAND gates.

**Magnetic storage** — hard disk drives and tape — works mechanically. A **disc spins** at high speed while a **read-write head** moves across its surface, **magnetising** tiny areas in one direction or the other to represent 0s and 1s. Reading detects the direction of magnetisation.

**Optical storage** — CD, DVD and Blu-ray — uses a **laser**. Data is stored as microscopic **pits** in the disc surface, with flat areas between them called **lands**; the pits are pressed in at the factory, or made by the laser on a recordable disc. Reading shines a laser at the surface and detects the difference in how pits and lands **reflect** the light, which is interpreted as 0s and 1s.

**Comparing them**, almost every difference traces back to the mechanism. Solid state is the **fastest**, most **durable**, quietest and lowest-power, all because it has **no moving parts** — nothing must spin up or move into position, and nothing can be damaged by a knock. Magnetic is **slower** and more fragile because of those moving parts, but is the **cheapest per gigabyte** and offers the **largest capacities**, which keeps it in use for bulk storage and backups. Optical holds the **least** and scratches easily, but discs are extremely cheap and highly portable, which suits distributing media.

So the right choice depends on what is being optimised: speed and durability point to solid state, capacity for the money to magnetic, and cheap distribution to optical.

questions.prompt: A small company is deciding whether to store its files on local drives in the office or in cloud storage. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each and give a justified recommendation.
questions.solution:
It is worth being clear first about what **cloud storage** actually is. It uses **magnetic and/or solid state storage at a remote location**, reached over a network. It is not a different kind of storage technology — it is the same hardware, owned and run by somebody else.

**Advantages of cloud storage for this company.** Staff could reach files from **any device, anywhere** with a connection, which matters if anyone works from home or visits customers. Files are **easy to share**, both internally and with clients, without emailing copies around. The provider handles **backups** and replaces failed drives, which a small company with no IT staff would otherwise have to do itself — and in practice often would not. Capacity can be **increased** immediately without buying hardware, so the company does not have to predict its needs in advance.

**Disadvantages.** The obvious one is that an **internet connection** is required: if the office connection fails, nobody can reach anything, and the business stops. Less obviously, access is limited by **connection speed**, which is far slower than a local drive — so working on large files is noticeably slower than opening them locally. The cost is **ongoing**, a subscription that continues indefinitely, rather than buying a drive once. And the data sits on **hardware owned and controlled by someone else**, so the company is trusting that provider's security, its staff, and its continued existence with confidential business information.

**Advantages of local storage** are the mirror image. Access is **fast**, because the drive is on the premises. There is **no ongoing fee** after the hardware is bought. The company keeps **full control** of its own data, which may matter for confidential records. The disadvantages are that **backups are the company's own responsibility** — and a fire, flood or theft could destroy both the working copy and the backup if they are kept in the same building — remote access is difficult, and adding capacity means buying and installing more hardware.

**Recommendation.** I would use **both**, rather than choosing one. Day-to-day working files should sit on **local storage**, so that everyday access is fast and work can continue if the internet connection drops. The company should then use **cloud storage for backups**, because that keeps a copy **physically away from the office** and so protects against fire, flood or theft — the single biggest weakness of a purely local arrangement.

If the company must choose only one, the deciding factor is the nature of the data. Where the files are highly confidential and the office connection is unreliable, **local** is safer. Where staff work in several places and there is nobody to manage backups, **cloud** is the better risk, because a small company that never gets round to backing up will eventually lose everything.

**Advantages of cloud storage for this company.** Staff could reach files from **any device, anywhere** with a connection, which matters if anyone works from home or visits customers. Files are **easy to share**, both internally and with clients, without emailing copies around. The provider handles **backups** and replaces failed drives, which a small company with no IT staff would otherwise have to do itself — and in practice often would not. Capacity can be **increased** immediately without buying hardware, so the company does not have to predict its needs in advance.

**Disadvantages.** The obvious one is that an **internet connection** is required: if the office connection fails, nobody can reach anything, and the business stops. Less obviously, access is limited by **connection speed**, which is far slower than a local drive — so working on large files is noticeably slower than opening them locally. The cost is **ongoing**, a subscription that continues indefinitely, rather than buying a drive once. And the data sits on **hardware owned and controlled by someone else**, so the company is trusting that provider's security, its staff, and its continued existence with confidential business information.

**Advantages of local storage** are the mirror image. Access is **fast**, because the drive is on the premises. There is **no ongoing fee** after the hardware is bought. The company keeps **full control** of its own data, which may matter for confidential records. The disadvantages are that **backups are the company's own responsibility** — and a fire, flood or theft could destroy both the working copy and the backup if they are kept in the same building — remote access is difficult, and adding capacity means buying and installing more hardware.

**Recommendation.** I would use **both**, rather than choosing one. Day-to-day working files should sit on **local storage**, so that everyday access is fast and work can continue if the internet connection drops. The company should then use **cloud storage for backups**, because that keeps a copy **physically away from the office** and so protects against fire, flood or theft — the single biggest weakness of a purely local arrangement.

If the company must choose only one, the deciding factor is the nature of the data. Where the files are highly confidential and the office connection is unreliable, **local** is safer. Where staff work in several places and there is nobody to manage backups, **cloud** is the better risk, because a small company that never gets round to backing up will eventually lose everything.

examTechnique.body:
Give **both** halves of the definition: **non-volatile** and **not directly accessible by the CPU**. For "explain the operation", describe the **mechanism** — pits and lands, a magnetised spinning disc, electrical circuits.

Trace advantages back to **no moving parts**. Say cloud storage is **magnetic and/or solid state at a remote location**, and define embedded by **one dedicated task**.
examinerErrors: Defining secondary storage only as "it keeps data when switched off".
Naming the component instead of describing how it works.
Writing about NAND gates, which are explicitly not required.
Treating cloud storage as a fourth type of storage.
Giving "you need internet" as the only cloud disadvantage.
Claiming solid state is better than magnetic in every respect.
Defining an embedded system as simply "a small computer".
Forgetting data must be copied into main memory before use.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives **both halves** of the secondary storage definition and can use the second half to explain why **ROM is not** secondary storage. It describes each mechanism physically — **pits and lands** read by reflection, a **head magnetising a spinning disc**, **electrical circuits** — and then derives the advantages from them, noting that speed, durability, silence and low power all follow from **no moving parts**. It states that cloud storage is **magnetic or solid state at a remote location**, gives disadvantages beyond connectivity — **connection speed**, **ongoing cost**, **someone else's hardware** — and concedes that **magnetic remains cheapest per gigabyte**. It defines embedded by **dedicated purpose**, not by size.
